organization: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Metropolitan Chicago
program: One-to-one volunteer mentoring for children aged 7 through high school

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/evidence-tier-batch-20261018/bbbs-chicago/acceptance.md — separately timed same-model source and model audit; not an independent second agent.

priceScope: Whole-organization cost per match against long-run earnings from the BBBS mentoring trial follow-up (Chicago not a trial site); income-only welfare comparison, not a verified marginal gift offer

what: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Metropolitan Chicago matches children from age seven through high school graduation with screened volunteer mentors, with staff monitoring each match.
It served 1,935 young people in 2025 after growing 37%, and holds events to take children off its waitlist for a mentor.
This in-depth review prices the organization’s whole cost per match against long-run earnings from a tax-record follow-up of Big Brothers Big Sisters’ randomized trial in eight other cities.
strengths: The 1991–93 randomized trial of about 1,100 youth found behavior improvements while matched; linked tax records show treatment youth were significantly more likely to attend college.
A larger observational comparison of unmatched applicants found earnings about 19% higher at ages 20 to 25, and Arnold Ventures rates community-based mentoring Near Top Tier.
Volunteers provide the mentoring, so cash costs are low: about $4,000 per young person a year.
reservations: Our working estimate is about $997K per better life; all of it is income, and the randomized trial’s own earnings estimate is imprecise.
Chicago was not a trial site, so we discount the transfer of results more heavily.
The cost per youth mixes the FY2023 budget with an estimate of 2024 youth served; current costs may differ after rapid growth.

sections.what: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Metropolitan Chicago (EIN 36-2681212) recruits, screens and trains adult volunteers ("Bigs") and matches them one-to-one with children ("Littles") from age seven through high school graduation, with professional staff monitoring each match. It serves the Chicago metropolitan area. It reported serving 1,935 young people in 2025, up 37%. A donation supports the whole organization.
sections.monitoring: The evidence comes from Big Brothers Big Sisters of America’s randomized waitlist trial at eight other agencies in 1991–93 (1,138 consenting families), linked by Bell and Petkova to tax records for 883 participants, and a 2025 observational extension using Boston applicants. The Chicago agency reports youth served on its website and, in 2021, reported 1,185 new matches under one grant. We did not find match durations or cost per match; we have not contacted the organization.
sections.qualitative: Within 18 months, the original trial found lower absenteeism and fewer school suspensions among matched youth. The long-run follow-up finds treatment youth significantly more likely to attend college, with imprecise earnings effects in the RCT itself. Comparing matched with unmatched applicants, it finds about 19% higher earnings at ages 20 to 25, and the Policy Impacts library records an estimated $56,000 lifetime earnings gain and a negative net government cost. Average adult wages in the sample were low ($16,500 for men, $14,000 for women at ages 25 to 30).
sections.cost:
Our central estimate is **$997K per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. It is an income-only comparison: we credit no health gain.

**Cost.** FY2023 (June) expense was $5.6M. Dividing by about 1,412 youth served in 2024 (implied by 1,935 in 2025 after 37% growth) gives about $3,970 per young person a year, or $5,956 per match at 1.5 years. The trial agencies spent about $2,778 per active match in 2018 dollars.

**Benefit.** We credit an 8% gross earnings gain on a $20,000 base from age 20 for 25 years, 60% as net welfare: under half the observational 19%, because the RCT’s earnings estimate is imprecise. We keep 0.5 for causality, 0.5 for transfer to a non-trial agency today, 0.9 for displacement and 0.8 for Chicago residence.

**Range.** At the trial’s cost the estimate is $886K per better life. Treating the 19% effect as fully causal gives $216K per better life; a 3% effect gives $2.62M per better life; gains lasting only ten years give $2.03M per better life. If there is no lasting earnings effect, there is no credited benefit.
sections.funding: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Metropolitan Chicago reported FY2023 (June) revenue of $5.9M, almost all contributions, and expenses of $5.6M, up from $5.3M in FY2022 and $5.1M in FY2021. Program expenses were $4.2M in FY2023. A match also needs a volunteer, so whether money alone adds matches is unverified.

model.costScope: FY2023 whole-organization expense per young person served (2024 estimate) × 1.5 years per match.
model.geographicAttribution: Chicago-area children; 0.8 of adult earning years in the Chicago metro.
model.formula: Price = 10 × cost per match ÷ [0.5 × discounted years(25, from age 20) × ln(1 + 0.6 × 8% × base ÷ base) × causal × transfer × non-displacement × Chicago share]. Health = 0.
model.attribution: A gift is credited with the average effect of an added match at whole-organization cost; volunteer supply is a binding constraint not modeled.
model.uncertainty: Dominated by whether the observational earnings effect is causal and how long it lasts, then transfer to school-based matches.
model.nativeOutcomes: College attendance, adult earnings (ages 20–30), incarceration, teen birth from tax and vital records.

scenarios.assumptions: FY2023 (June) expense over about 1,412 youth served in 2024 (1,935 in 2025 after 37% growth), times 1.5 years per match; 8% gross earnings gain from age 20 for 25 years on a $20,000 base; 0.5 causal, 0.5 transfer, 0.9 non-displacement, 0.8 Chicago residence.

incomePathways.rationale: Long-run tax-record follow-up of the 1991-93 eight-site BBBS randomized trial (Chicago was not a site): college attendance significantly higher; earnings effects imprecise in the RCT, about 19% at ages 20-25 in a larger observational comparison. Credited as an 8% gross gain from age 20 for 25 years, half treated as causal, net of taxes and lost benefits.
incomePathways.counterfactual: Randomized waitlisted youth (18 months) and, in the observational design, applicants who were never matched.
